name: Azelaic acid 15% (Finacea/Skinoren)

lead: Azelaic acid is a dicarboxylic acid used on the skin. The 15% gel (Finacea) is a prescription treatment for the inflamed bumps of rosacea, and a 20% cream (Skinoren) is used for acne. It also lightens dark patches, so it is used on melasma and post-inflammatory marks.

For looks, the payoff is fewer red bumps and pustules, calmer-looking skin and more even tone. Phase III trials showed the gel beat vehicle for inflamed rosacea lesions, and a network meta-analysis ranked it among effective topical options.

paras: It is applied as a thin layer to the affected facial skin, in a gel for rosacea or cream for acne, usually over months with a clinician's direction. It is often used alongside gentle skin care and sun protection.

The most reported effect is local skin irritation, such as stinging, burning and dryness, especially in sensitive or eczema-prone skin. In a network meta-analysis the 15% gel showed a higher adverse event odds ratio than other topicals.

chain: Reduces inflammation, bacteria and melanin synthesis
Fewer bumps, less redness, more even tone
angle.text: Used on the face for rosacea and acne, azelaic acid lessens inflamed lesions and redness and can fade dark marks, giving clearer, more even skin.

lead: Azelaic acid is a naturally occurring dicarboxylic acid used in dermatology. The 15% gel (Finacea) is approved for papulopustular rosacea and the 20% cream (Skinoren) is used for acne [1][2]. It is also used to lighten pigmented areas in melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, including as an alternative to hydroquinone [1].

The appearance goal is clearer, less red and more even skin on the face. Azelaic acid has antibacterial action against acne-associated bacteria, normalizes follicular keratinization, reduces inflammation and inhibits tyrosinase, which lowers melanin production [1].
Rosacea reviews place azelaic acid 15% gel among first-tier topical agents shown to reduce inflammatory lesions and erythema [3].

paras: It is used for facial hyperpigmentation such as melasma, where reviews describe treatment as challenging [4], and to even skin tone in darker skin types [1].

The 15% gel is used for papulopustular rosacea [1][2][3], and the 20% cream for mild-to-moderate acne, including in adult women, where a study of 251 women assessed severity and quality of life [5]. A pilot study compared it with anthralin in patchy alopecia areata [6].

Two vehicle-controlled randomized phase III studies evaluated the 15% gel for papulopustular rosacea [7]. A trial compared once- with twice-daily application [8]. A systematic review and network meta-analysis of 19 RCTs (8,208 participants) of moderate-to-severe papulopustular rosacea found azelaic acid 20% had the highest effect size, with 15%, metronidazole 0.75% and ivermectin 1% showing comparable effects [9]. Real-world data on the 15% gel's lesion reduction were also published [10]. A cost-effectiveness analysis compared rosacea therapies including azelaic acid [11].

Skin dryness and irritation are possible, especially in some people with eczema [1]. In the network meta-analysis, azelaic acid 15% had a statistically significant odds ratio for adverse events (1.95) versus other topical agents [9]. A 40-week investigator-blinded comparison of ivermectin cream and azelaic acid gel examined long-term safety [12].
Azelaic acid inhibits cathelicidin expression and the protease activity that cleaves it into LL-37, a peptide implicated in rosacea [10]. It also inhibits tyrosinase [1].

Evidence includes randomized phase III trials, a dosing-frequency trial, a 40-week safety trial, a network meta-analysis and real-world data in rosacea [7][8][9][10][12], and a non-interventional study of 20% cream in adult acne [5].
